title: What security training, drills and exercises does the ISPS Code require for ships and port facilities?
seoTitle: ISPS Code security training and drills
description: ISPS Code training for ship, company and port facility security officers, three-monthly drills and annual exercises, with US rules, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: The International Maritime Organization's ISPS Code requires company, ship and port facility security officers to have knowledge and training, personnel with security duties to be able to perform them, and drills and exercises at appropriate intervals. Part B guidance sets drills at least every three months and exercises at least once each calendar year with no more than 18 months between them. The United States makes those frequencies binding in 33 CFR parts 104 and 105.
keyTakeaways: The ISPS Code entered into force under SOLAS chapter XI-2 on July 1, 2004; Part A is mandatory and Part B is guidance on how to meet it.
Section 13 of Part A covers training, drills and exercises on ship security, and section 18 covers the same for port facilities.
Part B paragraph 13.6 adds a drill within one week when more than 25 percent of a ship's personnel change at once with people who have not drilled on that ship in the last 3 months.
The European Union, through Regulation (EC) No 725/2004, and the United States, through 33 CFR 104.230 and 105.220, both make the drill and exercise frequencies binding.
US rules require training, drill and exercise records to be kept for at least 2 years and require Vessel Security Officers on STCW ships to hold a Coast Guard endorsement.
jurisdiction: International (IMO), with European Union and United States (federal) implementation
regulator: International Maritime Organization (IMO); United States Coast Guard (USCG); EU Member State maritime security authorities
appliesTo: Company security officers and shore-based company personnel with security responsibilities
Ship security officers and shipboard personnel with specific security duties
All other shipboard personnel, who must be familiar with relevant parts of the ship security plan
Port facility security officers, facility personnel with security duties and all other facility personnel

sections.heading: What is the ISPS Code and who does it cover?

blocks.text: The International Ship and Port Facility Security (ISPS) Code is the IMO's mandatory security regime for international shipping. According to [IMO](https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/Security/Pages/SOLAS-XI-2%20ISPS%20Code.aspx), it entered into force under SOLAS chapter XI-2 on July 1, 2004. Part A sets mandatory requirements for governments, port authorities and shipping companies; Part B provides recommendatory guidelines on how to meet them.

The Code works through three designated security roles: the Company Security Officer (CSO), the Ship Security Officer (SSO) and the Port Facility Security Officer (PFSO). Each must assess risk, prepare a security plan and implement it. Training is the mechanism that makes the plan real for everyone else on the ship or facility.

This page covers the ISPS training and drill obligations. Seafarer security certification is set separately under STCW chapter VI; STCW security awareness training, which forms part of basic safety certification in Australia, is summarized on the [STCW page](/regulations/stcw-seafarer-training-requirements).

sections.heading: What do sections 13 and 18 of Part A require?

blocks.text: Section 13, "Training, drills and exercises on ship security", has five mandatory paragraphs. Section 18 mirrors it for port facilities. The Code text is reproduced in the annexes to [Regulation (EC) No 725/2004](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32004R0725).

items: **13.1:** the CSO and appropriate shore-based personnel shall have knowledge and have received training, taking into account Part B.
**13.2:** the SSO shall have knowledge and have received training, taking into account Part B.
**13.3:** shipboard personnel with specific security duties shall understand their responsibilities under the ship security plan and have sufficient knowledge and ability to perform them.
**13.4:** drills shall be carried out at appropriate intervals, taking into account ship type, personnel changes, port facilities to be visited and other circumstances.
**13.5:** the CSO shall ensure effective coordination and implementation of ship security plans by participating in exercises at appropriate intervals.

**18.1 to 18.4:** the PFSO and facility security personnel shall have knowledge and training, facility personnel with security duties shall be able to perform them, drills shall be carried out at appropriate intervals, and the PFSO shall participate in exercises.

blocks.text: Part A says "appropriate intervals" and points to Part B for the detail. That is why the Part B numbers below matter, and why jurisdictions that make them binding produce firmer audit expectations.

sections.heading: What training content and frequencies does Part B set?

blocks.text: Part B paragraph 13.1 lists 20 subjects for the CSO, shore-based staff and SSO, from security administration and ship security assessment methodology to recognition of weapons and dangerous substances, instruction techniques, and assessment of drills and exercises. Paragraph 13.2 adds five SSO-specific subjects, including ship layout, the ship security plan with scenario-based training, crowd management and testing of security equipment.

Paragraph 13.3 sets eleven areas for shipboard personnel with specific security duties, and paragraph 13.4 sets five areas that all other shipboard personnel should know, including the meaning of the different security levels and the emergency procedures and contingency plans. That tiered structure maps directly onto a [role-based training](/glossary/role-based-training) design.

blocks.title: Part B frequencies
blocks.text: Ship drills at least once every three months, plus a drill within one week whenever more than 25 percent of the ship's personnel has changed at one time with people who have not drilled on that ship in the last 3 months (13.6). Ship exercises at least once each calendar year with no more than 18 months between them (13.7). Port facility drills at least every three months unless specific circumstances dictate otherwise (18.5) and port facility exercises on the same annual and 18 month basis (18.6).

Exercises test communications, coordination, resource availability and response, and may be full scale or live, tabletop simulations or seminars, or combined with other exercises. A [tabletop exercise](/guides/how-to-run-a-tabletop-exercise) is therefore an accepted format, provided it genuinely tests the plan.

sections.heading: Where are the Part B frequencies binding?

blocks.text: In the European Union they are binding by regulation. Article 3(5) of Regulation (EC) No 725/2004 requires Member States to conform to listed Part B paragraphs "as if they were mandatory", including 13.6 and 13.7 (frequency of security drills and exercises for ships' crews and for company and ship security officers) and 18.5 and 18.6 (frequency of drills and exercises in port facilities and for PFSOs).

The same Article required Member States to apply the SOLAS special measures and Part A in full to international shipping by July 1, 2004 and to Class A passenger ships on domestic services by July 1, 2005. The Regulation does not apply to cargo ships under 500 gross tonnage, fishing vessels or vessels not engaged in commercial activities, among others.

sections.heading: How does the United States apply ISPS training and drills?

blocks.text: The Maritime Transportation Security Act regulations in 33 CFR part 104 (vessels) and part 105 (facilities) turn the ISPS training tiers into binding rules. A Vessel Security Officer must have general knowledge through training or equivalent job experience in listed subjects under [33 CFR 104.215](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-33/section-104.215). For seagoing vessels subject to STCW, the VSO must hold a Coast Guard credential with a VSO endorsement, which requires being at least 18, completing a Coast Guard-accepted VSO course and having at least 12 months of approved sea service (or 6 months plus knowledge of vessel operations).

Under [33 CFR 104.230](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-33/section-104.230), the VSO must ensure at least one security drill every 3 months, with a drill within one week of reactivation after a repair or seasonal lay-up, and a drill within one week whenever personnel with no prior drill participation on that vessel exceed 25 percent. Exercises must take place at least once each calendar year with no more than 18 months between them. [33 CFR 105.220](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-33/section-105.220) sets the same drill and exercise cycle for facilities, and a facility cannot require a moored vessel to take part in its drill.

Records are prescriptive. [33 CFR 104.235](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-33/section-104.235) and [33 CFR 105.225](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-33/section-105.225) require at least 2 years of records, including for each training session the date, duration, description and list of attendees, and for each drill or exercise the date, description, participants and any lessons learned. US rules also require personnel with security duties to maintain a Transportation Worker Identification Credential (TWIC) and to know the relevant parts of the TWIC program.

blocks.text: Storing these records against each person, rather than only against the ship, makes the 25 percent crew-change trigger easy to test. The guide on [preparing training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit) covers record structure.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry structures the ISPS Part B subject lists as knowledge points tied to each security role, and links drills and exercises to the plan elements they test. That lets a security officer see which plan elements have not been drilled this quarter and which crew members joined since the last drill.

faqs.q: Are ISPS Code drill frequencies mandatory?
faqs.a: Part A requires drills and exercises at appropriate intervals, and the specific frequencies sit in Part B guidance. The European Union makes Part B paragraphs 13.6, 13.7, 18.5 and 18.6 binding through Regulation (EC) No 725/2004, and the United States sets the same frequencies in 33 CFR 104.230 and 105.220.

faqs.q: Can a real increase in security level count as a drill?
faqs.a: In the United States, yes. Under 33 CFR 104.230 and 105.220, a drill or exercise requirement may be satisfied by implementing the security measures required by the plan following an increase in MARSEC Level, provided the vessel or facility reports attainment to the cognizant Captain of the Port.

faqs.q: How long must US vessel security training records be kept?
faqs.a: At least 2 years. Under 33 CFR 104.235, the Vessel Security Officer must keep records of training, including the date, duration, description and attendees of each session, and of each drill and exercise, and make them available to the Coast Guard on request.

faqs.q: Does a tabletop exercise satisfy the annual ISPS exercise?
faqs.a: It can. Part B and the US rules both allow exercises to be full scale or live, tabletop simulations or seminars, or combined with other exercises. Each exercise must still test communications, coordination, resource availability and response.
